boundary_note: Bounded first pass for Bodart's Boldekow entry (capitulation, 30 October 1806) in cohort v1's fourth-coalition 1806 group: the artillery park that Blücher had brought round the Harz, under Major Höpfner, from its march from Friedland to Boldekow on the morning of the 30th to its capitulation there through an officer sent by Marshal Lannes. The park's march from Breddin and Stüdenitz is context; the 60 mounted gunners brought in by a party of Murat's, reported in his letter of the 31st, are not added. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.value: Bodart prints no strength for either side. He has the French under Marshal Lannes (side A, French) force the escort of Blücher's artillery park under Major v. Höpfner (side B, Prussian) to capitulate, after which 25 guns, 48 ammunition wagons and 800 horses fell into the enemy's hands and about 600 men into captivity (claim side-b-losses). By his stated rule his figures are the forces available for the engagement, rounded up.
claims.rationale: Bodart's printed entry, read from the page image in the frame transcription; one claim among several. Höpfner and the French letters give other accounts of the park and of who was in it (claims side-b-strength, side-b-strength-french). English rendering (ours) of Bodart's rules: p. 46, 'the strengths given are always those forces that were disposable for the battle'; p. 47, 'the strength and loss figures were rounded up by the author'. English rendering (ours) of the heading and entry: '1806 30/10. capitulation of Boldekow'; 'the French under Marshal Lannes force the escort of Blücher's artillery park under Major v. Höpfner to capitulate, after which 25 guns, 48 ammunition wagons, 800 horses fell into the hands of the enemy and about 600 men into captivity'.

citations.quote: 1806 30./10. KAPITULATION von Boldekow

Die Franzosen unter Marschall Lannes nötigen die Bedeckungsmannschaft des Blücher'schen Artillerieparks unter Major v. Höpfner zur Kapitulation, wonach 25 Kanonen, 48 Munitionswägen, 800 Pferde in die Hände des Feindes und ca. 600 M. in Kriegsgefangenschaft gerieten.

claims.value: Side B (Prussian) in Höpfner: the artillery park that General Blücher had brought round the Harz reached Breddin and Stüdenitz on 24 October under an escort of 24 cuirassiers of the Heising regiment; at Rheinsberg the artillery lieutenant Westphal joined it with 6 train and bread wagons and 250 horses, and at Friedland Lieutenant Streit's park column No. 5 with 24 more vehicles, much baggage and an infantry detachment of 100 men. The infantry escort and the few cuirassiers declared that no resistance could be expected of them, men and horses being too exhausted, and the escort was far too small for so long a column of wagons. By the time of the capitulation the whole escort had gone off to save itself across the Peene; 14 officers, 250 artillerymen, 300 drivers and about 800 horses were handed over with 25 guns and 48 ammunition wagons.
claims.rationale: Side B's history, read from the page images of pp. 233-236. The column was brought from the retreat, so the claim is tagged inherited. The men handed over total 564 (our arithmetic). Bodart's 'escort' (Bedeckungsmannschaft) is not Höpfner's: in Höpfner the escort had left, and the men handed over were the park's officers, artillerymen and drivers. English renderings (ours): 'the artillery park, which General Blücher had led so happily round the Harz and so particularly commended to Colonel Massenbach at the meeting in Neustadt on the Dosse, had on the'; '24th of October, under the escort of 24 cuirassiers of the regiment Heising, reached the villages of Breddin and Stüdenitz, between Havelberg and Kyritz, to hold a rest day there by order of Prince Hohenlohe, reach Rheinsberg in 2 days and await further orders'; 'after the artillery lieutenant Westphal had joined him with 6 train and bread wagons and 250 horses'; 'at Friedland park column No. 5 of Lieutenant Streit joined the artillery column with another 24 vehicles, much baggage and an infantry detachment of 100 men'; 'the infantry escort, like the few cuirassiers, declared that no resistance was to be expected of them, as men and horses were too exhausted; this escort was also far too small for a column of wagons of such great length to protect it even in more favourable circumstances'; 'it was believed that under these circumstances a capitulation had to be made, and there were handed over to the enemy 25 guns, 48 ammunition wagons, spare carriages etc., 14 officers, 250 artillerymen, 300 drivers and about 800 horses'; 'the whole escort had gone off to save itself across the Peene'. 'ꝛc.' is the print's abbreviation for 'etc.'.

claims.value: Side B (Prussian), side A's (French) figures: Lannes wrote to the Emperor on 31 October that 1,500 men, almost all artillery, 200 dragoons, 30 guns, 60 caissons and many wagons full of munitions, all well horsed, had surrendered the day before to his outposts. Murat wrote the same day that he had met the great artillery park, which had surrendered to an officer of Lannes's, 1 league from Friedland, and that a party scouting his left had brought in 60 mounted gunners on their way to join it.
claims.rationale: Side A's figures, read from the page images; not reconciled with Höpfner's or Bodart's (claims side-b-strength, bodart-strength). Lannes's further letter from Pasewalk repeats figures for the park and its gunners, seen only in the OCR and not restated. The column was brought from the retreat, so the claim is tagged inherited. English renderings (ours): Lannes, 'Marshal Lannes to the Emperor. Pasewalk, 31 October 1806'; 'I have the honour to inform Your Majesty that 1,500 men, almost all of the artillery, 200 dragoons, 30 guns, 60 caissons and many wagons filled with munitions, all well horsed, surrendered yesterday to my outposts. I am having all of it filed off to Spandau'; Murat, 'the Grand Duke of Berg to the Emperor. Friedland, 31 October 1806, 6 o'clock in the evening'; 'this morning, 1 league from Friedland, I met the great artillery park, which had surrendered to an officer of Marshal Lannes, and a party of a few men who were scouting my left brought us 60 mounted gunners who were going to join this same park, which is directed on Stettin'.

claims.value: Side A (French): Bodart names only the French under Marshal Lannes. Lannes says the park surrendered to his outposts, and Murat that it surrendered to an officer of Lannes's. In Höpfner, Lieutenant Braun II met the enemy at Neuensund, 1¼ miles short of Strasburg, and Lannes, who had gone to Pasewalk in person, sent him back to Boldekow with a French officer to negotiate. A party of a few men scouting Murat's left brought in 60 mounted gunners. No passage read gives the strength of the French troops to whom the park surrendered.

claims.value: Höpfner: when Lieutenant Braun II, met at Neuensund, gave himself out as a parlementaire, he was sent to Marshal Lannes at Pasewalk, who had gone there in person and sent him back to Boldekow with a French officer to negotiate with the commanding officer. Lannes wrote that the park surrendered to his outposts and that he was having it all filed off to Spandau; Murat, that it had surrendered to an officer of Lannes's. claims.value: Höpfner: Major Höpfner led the artillery column, which Blücher had urged to make particular haste. At Rheinsberg, when Prince Hohenlohe's expected orders failed to come and news arrived of a fight of Blücher's rear guard, he judged it unwise either to march on Fürstenberg or to spend the night at Rheinsberg, and marched by Alt-Strelitz towards Woldeck; at Bredenfelde, hearing that Pasewalk was in the enemy's hands, he turned to Friedland. There he told General Bila I that he meant to follow him to Anklam the next day, but Bila sent word that he should not march to Anklam but take his measures at his own discretion. In great perplexity the major called all the officers together to decide where to turn if they could march neither to Anklam nor to Stettin, and they resolved to march to Boldekow for forage. There, hearing that the enemy was pushing into Mecklenburg, they sent Lieutenant Braun II with a trumpeter towards Pasewalk to see how far the enemy had come; when the French officer came back with him, it was thought that a capitulation had to be made. Höpfner adds that no one thought of destroying the artillery material or of saving the men on the horses still found fit.
claims.rationale: Side B's history, read from the page images of pp. 234-236. Höpfner does not name his sources, and the passive 'man glaubte' does not say who decided to capitulate. English renderings (ours): 'on the 26th the artillery thus reached the village of Wildberg by Wusterhausen, and marched on the 27th in the night through Neu-Ruppin to Rheinsberg, as General Blücher had particularly urged haste on the leader of the artillery column, Major Höpfner, during the march through Gantzer'; 'when at Rheinsberg the expected orders of Prince Hohenlohe failed to come, and towards evening the news of a fight of General Blücher's rear guard also came in, Major Höpfner did not think it advisable to march on Fürstenberg as well, nor yet to spend the night at Rheinsberg, but, after the artillery lieutenant Westphal had also joined him with 6 train and bread wagons and 250 horses, he set out at half past 8 in the evening and marched to Alt-Strelitz, where he arrived on the morning of the 28th at half past 5, had the horses fed there and continued the march in the direction of Woldeck'; 'at 5 o'clock in the evening he reached Bredenfelde (8¼ miles from Rheinsberg), where he received the news that Pasewalk was already in the hands of the enemy, so that the road to Strasburg could no longer properly be taken'; 'the artillery therefore marched on the morning of the 29th on Friedland (4 miles), where it arrived at 5 o'clock in the evening'; 'Major Höpfner there also spoke with General Bila I, who was about to go to Anklam, and told him that it was his intention to march there as well the next day. It was not long, however, before General Bila sent back and had the major told that he should not march to Anklam, but take his measures at his discretion'; 'Major Höpfner was in great perplexity about what to do next, and assembled all the officers to deliberate where to turn if they could march neither to Anklam nor to Stettin'; 'it was therefore decided to march first, on the morning of the 30th, to the nearest Prussian village, Boldekow, so as at least to get forage'; 'in Boldekow came the news that the enemy was pushing into Mecklenburg, which was confirmed by a patrol coming from Friedland'; 'Lieutenant Braun II of the artillery was now sent with a trumpeter in the direction of Pasewalk to see how far the enemy had advanced'; as in claim side-a-strength for his meeting with the enemy and the French officer; as in claim side-b-strength for the capitulation; 'no one thought of destroying the artillery material or of trying to save the men on the horses still found fit'.

Lannes wrote that the park surrendered to his outposts the day before his letter of 31 October; Murat, that it had surrendered to an officer of Lannes's.

claims.value: Side B's loss was the park. Höpfner: 25 guns, 48 ammunition wagons, spare carriages, 14 officers, 250 artillerymen, 300 drivers and about 800 horses handed over, the escort having gone off across the Peene. Bodart: 25 guns, 48 ammunition wagons and 800 horses taken and about 600 men made prisoner. Lannes: 1,500 men, almost all artillery, 200 dragoons, 30 guns, 60 caissons and many wagons of munitions surrendered to his outposts. Murat: 60 mounted gunners on their way to join the park were brought in by a party.
claims.rationale: Separate accounts read from the page images (Bodart's from the frame transcription), not combined. Bodart's guns, wagons and horses are Höpfner's figures, and his about 600 men are Höpfner's 564 rounded up (our arithmetic); which source Bodart used was not checked. claims.value: Bodart places Boldekow, a village in Pomerania, 14 km south of Anklam. Höpfner calls it the nearest Prussian village, to which the column marched from Friedland on the morning of the 30th; the column had come by Alt-Strelitz and Bredenfelde, 8¼ miles from Rheinsberg, and Friedland, 4 miles further; Lieutenant Braun II met the enemy at Neuensund, 1¼ miles short of Strasburg; the escort went off across the Peene. Murat met the park 1 league from Friedland on 31 October.
claims.rationale: Location and routes as described, read from the page images. English renderings (ours): Bodart, '(village in Prussia, Pomerania, 14 km south of Anklam)'; Höpfner, as in claims side-b-command for the march, Friedland, Boldekow and Lieutenant Braun's errand, side-a-strength for Neuensund and side-b-strength for the escort's flight; Murat, as in claim side-b-strength-french.

claims.value: Side B (Prussian): Höpfner says the column travelled with requisitioned teams as far as Rheinsberg, but the last of these horses had to be dismissed there for want of forage, scarcely any being found even for the artillery horses; in Mecklenburg no teams could be had, and the artillery horses were wholly overdriven and starved, so the march could only go slowly; little forage was found at Friedland, and the column marched to Boldekow at least to get forage. Side A (French): Lannes called the park all well horsed, and in a further letter its gunners almost all mounted and marching in the greatest order.
claims.rationale: Side B's state, brought from the retreat, from Höpfner's page images of pp. 234-235; Lannes's letters from the page image of p. 568 and the OCR of p. 597. Lannes's 'well horsed' and Höpfner's starved horses are kept as given. English renderings (ours): Höpfner, 'as far as Rheinsberg, which was reached on the 27th at 6 o'clock in the morning, everything had been driven in one stretch with requisitioned teams; but as the last horses had already been brought from Stüdenitz and had no more forage, they were obliged to dismiss them, because forage could scarcely be found for the artillery horses'; 'march could only advance slowly, as in Mecklenburg no requisitioned teams were to be had and the artillery horses were wholly overdriven and starved. In Friedland only a little forage could be found'; as in claim side-b-command for the march to Boldekow; Lannes, as in claims side-b-strength-french and side-a-command.

citations.quote: Der Major Höpfner sprach daselbst noch den General Bila I., der im Begriff war, nach Anklam zu gehen, und eröffnete ihm, daß es seine Absicht sei, am folgenden Tage ebenfalls dahin zu marschiren. Es dauerte indessen nicht lange, so sandte der General Bila zurück und ließ dem Major sagen: er möge nicht nach Anklam marschiren, sondern seine Maßregeln nach Gutdünken treffen.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 235 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Der Major Höpfner war in großer Verlegenheit was weiter zu thun sei, und versammelte die sämmtlichen Offiziere, um zu berathschlagen, wohin man sich zu wenden habe, wenn man weder nach Anklam, noch nach Stettin marschiren könne.

citations.quote: Man beschloß daher am 30. Morgens vorerst nach dem nächsten preußischen Dorf Boldekow zu marschiren, um wenigstens Futter zu erhalten.

claims.value: Side A (French) was advancing: at Boldekow the Prussians heard the enemy was pushing into Mecklenburg, their officer met the enemy at Neuensund, and Bodart has the French under Lannes force the capitulation. Side B did not resist: its escort declared no resistance could be expected and went off across the Peene, and the park capitulated to a French officer sent to negotiate.
claims.rationale: Coded A_attacked: side A was advancing on and pursuing side B, and side B made no resistance. The phase is left unresolved: the passages read do not show who set the French advance towards Boldekow, and the contact was made by the Prussian lieutenant sent out to reconnoitre. English renderings (ours): Höpfner, as in claims side-b-command for the news at Boldekow, side-a-strength for Neuensund and the French officer, and side-b-strength for the escort; Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength.

claims.value: The passages read name no works: the park stood in the village of Boldekow, to which it had marched for forage, and the French are described only at Neuensund and Pasewalk and as Lannes's outposts. No fighting took place.
claims.rationale: Coded none_named: the cited passages describe where both sides stood and name no fortification; the village was held without named works. English renderings (ours): Höpfner, as in claims side-b-command for the march to Boldekow and side-a-strength for Neuensund and Pasewalk; Lannes, as in claim side-b-strength-french.

open_questions: Deferred: the rest of Lannes's further letter from Pasewalk (Foucart t. II, pp. 597-598), read only in the OCR; a French return of the park and its prisoners; the records of the Prussian judicial inquiries held after the war, on which by the preface of his first volume Höpfner's work chiefly rests; whether the author Höpfner was related to the park's commander, Major Höpfner. Figures seen only in the OCR and not restated: Lannes's figures for the park, its teams and its gunners in that letter (p. 597).

Most consequential gap: who and how many side B were. Höpfner's men handed over were the park's 14 officers, 250 artillerymen and 300 drivers, 564 in all (our arithmetic), the escort having left; Bodart has the escort capitulate and about 600 men taken; Lannes has 1,500 men, almost all artillery, and 200 dragoons. Side A's force is not given at all. A French return of the prisoners, or Lannes's outpost reports, could settle both.

Disputes kept as separate claims: the men (564 from Höpfner's figures, by our arithmetic; about 600, Bodart; 1,500 and 200 dragoons, Lannes; Murat's 60 mounted gunners taken separately); the guns (25, Höpfner and Bodart; 30, Lannes); the wagons (48 ammunition wagons, Höpfner and Bodart; 60 caissons and many wagons, Lannes); whether the escort capitulated (Bodart) or had gone off across the Peene (Höpfner); the park's destination (Spandau, Lannes; Stettin, Murat); the state of its horses (starved, Höpfner; well horsed, Lannes).

Families and dependence: Bodart (a compilation; his sources for this entry were not checked, though his 25 guns, 48 wagons and 800 horses are Höpfner's figures and his about 600 men Höpfner's 564 rounded up, by our arithmetic); Foucart, t. II (the French side's documents: Lannes's and Murat's letters of 31 October from the page images, Lannes's further letter from the OCR); Höpfner, Bd. 2, 2nd edition (the Prussian side's history; by the preface of his first volume the work rests chiefly on the records of the judicial inquiries held after the war, but the Boldekow passage names no source).
